subject: Biology
title: Control and Coordination: Nerves, Hormones & Reflex Arcs
hook: Why does your hand pull away from fire before you even think? Meet Arjun as he learns how his brain and hormones control every move.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: curious student learning reflexes and hormones

characters.name: Dr. Sharma
characters.role: village doctor explaining the nervous system

slides.title: Control and Coordination
slides.storyContext: Arjun touches a hot pan accidentally. His hand jerks away instantly—before his brain even tells him it hurts. How?

image.alt: Control and Coordination — Control and Coordination

slides.title: The Reflex Moment
slides.storyContext: In his kitchen, Arjun burns his finger on a pan. His hand pulls back in less than a second. His mother rushes over, but he's already moved. Dr. Sharma visits that evening and explains: 'Your body has a shortcut—the reflex arc. It protects you faster than your brain can think.'

image.alt: The Reflex Moment — Control and Coordination

slides.title: The Nervous System Architecture
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma draws a diagram. 'Your nervous system has two main parts: the Central Nervous System, which is your command center, and the Peripheral Nervous System, which carries messages.'

points.label: Central Nervous System (CNS)
points.text: Brain and spinal cord. Integrates information, makes decisions, sends commands.

points.label: Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)
points.text: Nerves branching from brain and spinal cord to all body parts. Sensory nerves bring info in; motor nerves send commands out.

points.label: Somatic vs. Autonomic
points.text: Somatic nervous system: voluntary control (moving arm, walking). Autonomic nervous system: involuntary (heart rate, digestion, breathing).

example.problem: When you pick up a cold glass of water, is it under voluntary or involuntary control? Which nervous system division handles it?
example.solution: Voluntary control. The somatic (somatomotor) nervous system is responsible. Sensory neurons detect coldness; your brain sends motor signals to your hand muscles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your brain and spinal cord make decisions. Nerves carry signals to your muscles and organs like telephone wires carrying messages.

image.alt: The Nervous System Architecture — Control and Coordination

slides.title: Arjun's Nerve Discovery
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma traces a line down Arjun's spine. 'This white cord inside your spine—this is your spinal cord. It's part of your command center. When you burned your finger, signals raced up this cord to your brain, and orders raced back down. All in a blink.'

slides.title: Neurons: The Messengers
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'The smallest units in your nervous system are neurons. They're cells that send electrical and chemical signals.'

points.label: Neuron parts
points.text: Cell body (soma), dendrites (receive signals), and axon (send signals). Axon terminal releases neurotransmitters.

points.label: Action potential
points.text: When stimulated, a neuron's membrane potential changes from -70 mV (resting) to +30 mV (active), sending a signal down the axon.

points.label: Synapse
points.text: Gap between neurons. Neurotransmitter (acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, etc.) bridges the gap, turning one neuron's signal into the next neuron's input.

example.problem: A neurotransmitter is released but is not picked up by the next neuron. What happens?
example.solution: The signal stops. No action potential is triggered in the receiving neuron. Communication breaks down at that synapse.

slides.inSimpleWords: Neurons are nerve cells. They send electrical signals along their axon and use chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) to talk to the next neuron across a tiny gap called a synapse.

image.alt: Neurons: The Messengers — Control and Coordination

slides.title: How a Neuron Fires: The Pathway
slides.storyContext: Priya draws a neuron on the board. 'Watch how a signal travels: dendrite receives, cell body integrates, axon sends, synapse relays.'

example.problem: Trace the path of an electrical signal as it travels from a sensory neuron's dendrite, through its cell body, down its axon, and to a motor neuron.
example.solution: 1. Dendrite receives stimulus (sensory input). 2. Signal depolarizes the cell body. 3. If threshold is crossed, action potential fires. 4. Electrical signal propagates down the axon via ion channels. 5. Signal reaches axon terminal. 6. Neurotransmitters are released into synapse. 7. Neurotransmitters bind to receptors on motor neuron's dendrite. 8. Motor neuron depolarizes and fires (or inhibits, depending on neurotransmitter).

slides.title: The Reflex Arc
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma traces Arjun's burned finger. 'Your spinal cord didn't wait for your brain. It sensed danger and ordered your muscles to pull back. That's a reflex arc—the fastest path.'

points.label: Stimulus
points.text: Hot pan touches skin. Temperature receptors fire.

points.label: Sensory neuron
points.text: Carries signal from receptor (skin) → spinal cord.

points.label: Synapse in spinal cord
points.text: Sensory neuron connects to motor neuron (or relay neuron). Quick transfer of signal.

points.label: Motor neuron
points.text: Carries signal from spinal cord → muscle.

points.label: Response
points.text: Muscle contracts; hand pulls away. Brain receives the signal a moment later and perceives pain.

example.problem: A person's reflex to pull their hand away from a hot stove is intact, but they don't feel pain. Which part of the reflex arc is affected?
example.solution: The sensory relay to the brain is interrupted (perhaps spinal cord damage higher up or a neurological condition). The reflex arc from skin → spinal cord → muscle is intact, but the pathway from spinal cord → brain is blocked, so conscious pain perception doesn't occur.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reflex arc: Sense danger → send signal to spinal cord → spinal cord orders muscles to move → you move before you even feel pain.

image.alt: The Reflex Arc — Control and Coordination

slides.title: Why Reflexes Are Faster Than Thinking
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'My hand moved before I even felt pain. How is that possible?' Priya nods. 'The reflex arc bypasses your brain. Your spinal cord makes the decision alone. By the time your brain knows about the pain, your hand is already safe.'

slides.title: The Brain: Three Regions
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a side view of a brain. 'The brain is divided into three main parts, each with its own job.'

points.label: Forebrain (Cerebrum)
points.text: Cerebral cortex: thinking, learning, memory, voluntary movement, sensory perception (sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell). Largest and most complex.

points.label: Midbrain
points.text: Relay station between forebrain and hindbrain. Coordinates eye and ear movement.

points.label: Hindbrain (Cerebellum + Medulla)
points.text: Cerebellum: balance and coordination. Medulla: controls breathing, heart rate, blood pressure (vital functions).

example.problem: A person gets a stroke in their medulla. What vital functions are immediately at risk?
example.solution: Breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure control. The medulla controls these autonomic functions. Damage here is life-threatening.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your forebrain thinks and remembers. Your midbrain relays messages. Your hindbrain keeps you balanced and keeps your heart beating.

image.alt: The Brain: Three Regions — Control and Coordination

slides.title: Arjun's Brain in Action
slides.storyContext: At school, Arjun remembers the formula for photosynthesis. 'That's your cerebrum working,' Priya says. 'Yesterday, you learned it. Your cerebrum stored that memory. Today, you recalled it.'

slides.title: Brain Functions in Everyday Life
slides.storyContext: Priya describes a day in Arjun's life to show which brain region is active at each moment.

example.problem: Arjun wakes up, feels the blanket (sensory), climbs out of bed (motor control), remembers his exam today (memory), walks to school without falling (balance). Which brain region is responsible for each?
example.solution: Sensory perception (touch) → Forebrain (sensory cortex). Motor control (climbing) → Forebrain (motor cortex). Memory (exam) → Forebrain (hippocampus). Balance (not falling) → Hindbrain (cerebellum). Heart beating during walk → Hindbrain (medulla).

slides.title: Hormones: Chemical Messengers
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma shifts gears: 'Nerves are fast messengers. But long-term changes—growth, mood, metabolism—are controlled by slower, longer-lasting messengers called hormones.'

points.label: What is a hormone?
points.text: A chemical messenger produced by an endocrine gland, released into the bloodstream, travels to a target organ, and triggers a response.

points.label: Key hormones and glands
points.text: Insulin (pancreas, regulates blood glucose). Adrenaline (adrenal glands, fight-or-flight response). Growth hormone (pituitary, growth). Testosterone/Estrogen (testes/ovaries, sexual development).

points.label: Negative feedback
points.text: If blood glucose rises, pancreas releases insulin. Insulin lowers glucose. Once glucose is normal, pancreas stops. Maintains homeostasis.

example.problem: Arjun sees a snake near the well and his heart races, pupils dilate, and hands sweat. Which hormone is responsible?
example.solution: Adrenaline (epinephrine) from adrenal glands. It triggers the 'fight-or-flight' response: increased heart rate, dilated pupils, sweat glands activate, blood glucose rises for energy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hormones are chemical messages sent by glands into your blood. They travel slowly but reach distant organs and cause long-lasting changes like growth and mood.

image.alt: Hormones: Chemical Messengers — Control and Coordination

slides.title: Why Arjun Grew Taller This Year
slides.storyContext: Arjun notices his clothes are too small. 'Growth hormone!' Priya smiles. 'Your pituitary gland has been quietly releasing it. That hormone tells your bones and muscles to grow. Over weeks and months, you become taller.'

slides.title: Hormones vs. Nerves: Speed and Duration
slides.storyContext: Priya compares the two systems side-by-side to show why your body needs both.

example.problem: You touch a hot stove. Describe both the nervous system's response (within milliseconds) and the endocrine system's response (within minutes to hours).
example.solution: Nervous system (immediate): Pain signal travels via sensory neuron to spinal cord. Motor neuron fires. Hand pulls away in <1 second. Brain perceives pain. Endocrine system (delayed): Stress from pain triggers adrenal medulla to release adrenaline. Adrenaline increases heart rate and blood pressure over seconds to minutes. Over hours, cortisol is released for sustained stress response. Together: instant protection + sustained recovery.

slides.title: The Autonomic Nervous System
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma explains: 'Part of your nervous system works without you thinking about it. This is the autonomic nervous system. It has two branches: sympathetic and parasympathetic.'

points.label: Sympathetic nervous system
points.text: Fight-or-flight response. Increases heart rate, dilates pupils, redirects blood to muscles, inhibits digestion. Activated by stress or danger.

points.label: Parasympathetic nervous system
points.text: Rest-and-digest response. Decreases heart rate, constricts pupils, promotes digestion and absorption. Activated when relaxed or eating.

points.label: Balance
points.text: These two systems oppose each other, maintaining homeostasis. In normal conditions, parasympathetic dominates. During stress, sympathetic takes over.

example.problem: Arjun eats a meal. Which autonomic branch is active during digestion, and what does it do?
example.solution: Parasympathetic nervous system. It promotes saliva production, stomach acid secretion, and intestinal peristalsis (muscle contractions). Heart rate drops. Blood is diverted to the digestive organs. This is the 'rest-and-digest' state.

slides.inSimpleWords: The sympathetic nervous system says 'run!' in danger. The parasympathetic nervous system says 'relax' when safe. Your body switches between them.

slides.title: Integration: The Nervous and Endocrine Systems Working Together
slides.storyContext: Priya ties it together: 'Arjun, your nervous system and endocrine system work as a team. One is fast; one is long-lasting.'

points.label: Immediate response
points.text: Nervous system fires (milliseconds). Sympathetic branches activate.

points.label: Hormone release
points.text: Adrenal medulla (controlled by sympathetic nerves) releases adrenaline. Spread via bloodstream (seconds to minutes).

points.label: Sustained stress
points.text: Hypothalamus → pituitary → adrenal cortex releases cortisol for long-term stress adaptation (hours to days).

points.label: Recovery
points.text: Once threat passes, parasympathetic activates. Cortisol and adrenaline levels drop. Homeostasis restored.

slides.inSimpleWords: Nerves provide instant defense. Hormones keep the defense going. Together they keep you safe and balanced.

slides.title: Full Example: Exam Day Physiology
slides.storyContext: Priya uses Arjun's upcoming exam as a complete case study.

example.problem: It's exam day. Arjun feels nervous. His heart races, palms sweat, mind sharpens. Explain the role of nerves and hormones.
example.solution: 1. Brain perceives exam stress (cerebrum). 2. Sympathetic nervous system activates (from medulla and spinal cord). 3. Adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline. 4. Heart rate increases, blood diverts to muscles and brain, glucose is released, pupils dilate. 5. In the long term, if stress persists, cortisol (from adrenal cortex) increases, affecting metabolism and immunity. The nervous system gives immediate response; hormones sustain it.

image.alt: Full Example: Exam Day Physiology — Control and Coordination

slides.title: Challenge: The Diabetes Question
slides.storyContext: Arjun's grandmother eats a lot of jaggery and rice, but her body can't regulate her blood sugar. Dr. Sharma diagnoses type 2 diabetes.

example.problem: In type 2 diabetes, the pancreas produces insulin, but cells don't respond to it (insulin resistance). Blood glucose remains high. Which hormone is failing? Which organ is the target? What is the consequence?
example.solution: Insulin is produced by the pancreas's islet cells (beta cells) but is not working. The target organs (liver, muscle, fat cells) are resistant. Glucose cannot enter cells efficiently, so it accumulates in blood, causing hyperglycemia. This can damage blood vessels, kidneys, and nerves over time.

image.alt: Challenge: The Diabetes Question — Control and Coordination

slides.title: Challenge: A Broken Reflex Arc
slides.storyContext: A person with spinal cord damage can't pull their hand away from a hot stove, though they can still feel pain when the doctor tests their sensitivity.

example.problem: A person has partial spinal cord damage at the thoracic level (mid-back). They can feel pain and temperature in their hands, but their hand reflex when touching a hot object is absent. The sensory pathway works, but the motor response doesn't. Where is the damage: in the sensory neuron, the synapse in the spinal cord, or the motor neuron?
example.solution: The damage is in the motor neuron or the synapse in the spinal cord. The sensory neuron works (person feels pain). The damage interrupts the return pathway from spinal cord → muscle, so the reflex doesn't fire, even though the brain eventually receives the pain signal.

slides.title: Challenge: Neurotransmitter Imbalance
slides.storyContext: A person with depression has low levels of serotonin, a neurotransmitter that regulates mood.

example.problem: If serotonin is low at synapses in the brain, how would this affect mood and behavior? What does an antidepressant drug that blocks serotonin reuptake (prevents the neurotransmitter from being recycled) do to solve the problem?
example.solution: Low serotonin means fewer mood-regulating signals between neurons. This leads to depression, anxiety, and sleep disturbance. A reuptake inhibitor (like SSRIs) prevents the receiving neuron from absorbing serotonin, so serotonin stays in the synapse longer, strengthening the signal. More effective mood regulation results.

slides.title: Hormones in Puberty
slides.storyContext: Priya explains to the class. 'As teenagers, your endocrine system releases a surge of sex hormones—testosterone in boys, estrogen in girls. This is why you grow, develop, and feel new emotions.'

slides.title: Thyroid Hormone and Metabolism
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma describes. 'Your thyroid gland produces thyroid hormone. Too little, and you feel cold and sluggish. Too much, and you're anxious and energized. It controls how fast your body burns energy.'

example.problem: A person with an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) feels cold, tired, and gains weight. How does thyroid hormone control metabolism?
example.solution: Thyroid hormone increases the rate of cellular respiration in mitochondria. It tells cells to burn more glucose and fat for energy, releasing heat. With low thyroid hormone, respiration slows, less energy is released, body temperature drops, and metabolism slows—leading to weight gain.

slides.title: Challenge: Feedback Loops and Homeostasis
slides.storyContext: Arjun gets an infection. His immune system activates, raising body temperature to fight the pathogen.

example.problem: When body temperature rises due to infection, the body sets a new 'set point.' Explain negative feedback: how does the hypothalamus detect the high temperature, and what response brings it back to normal after the infection is defeated?
example.solution: 1. Hypothalamus detects elevated temperature via temperature-sensitive neurons. 2. Hypothalamus activates cooling mechanisms: sweating, vasodilation (blood vessels expand), reduced metabolism. 3. As body cools, temperature reaches normal set point. 4. Negative feedback: decreased temperature inhibits further cooling responses. 5. Parasympathetic nervous system dominates, heart rate and respiration return to baseline. Homeostasis restored.

slides.title: Arjun's Long Day
slides.storyContext: Priya summarizes Arjun's day through the lens of nervous and endocrine systems. 'Morning: adrenaline wakes you. School: acetylcholine helps you focus. Afternoon: fatigue from sustained cortisol. Evening: melatonin prepares you for sleep.'

slides.title: Challenge: Spinal Injuries and Motor Control
slides.storyContext: A person with a spinal cord injury at the neck can still blink and swallow (lower brainstem) but cannot move their legs (signals cannot pass spinal cord).

example.problem: Explain why a high spinal cord injury (cervical spine) paralyzes the legs but not the face or eyes. Which parts of the nervous system are still intact and functional?
example.solution: The brainstem and lower brain are unharmed, so control of face, eyes, tongue (via cranial nerves from brainstem) remains intact. The spinal cord damage interrupts the pathway from motor cortex (via spinal cord) to leg muscles. Lower brainstem + local spinal reflexes below injury remain functional (can still pull leg away from heat), but voluntary control from brain is lost. Spinal reflex arcs work independently of conscious control.

slides.title: Summary: Control and Coordination
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Dr. Sharma concludes: 'Every action, thought, and heartbeat is orchestrated by your nervous and endocrine systems.'

points.label: Nervous system
points.text: CNS (brain and spinal cord) + PNS (nerves). Fast communication via neurons and action potentials.

points.label: Reflex arc
points.text: Sensory → spinal cord → motor → response. Fastest protection path, bypasses conscious thought.

points.label: Brain regions
points.text: Cerebrum (thinking), midbrain (relay), cerebellum (balance), medulla (vital functions).

points.label: Neurons and synapses
points.text: Electrical and chemical signals travel neuron-to-neuron via neurotransmitters at synapses.

points.label: Autonomic balance
points.text: Sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) maintain homeostasis.

points.label: Hormones
points.text: Slow, long-lasting chemical messengers from endocrine glands. Regulate growth, metabolism, mood, reproduction.

points.label: Integration
points.text: Nervous system = fast response. Endocrine system = sustained response. Together they maintain homeostasis.

subject: Biology
title: How do Organisms Reproduce? Sexual & Asexual Pathways
hook: From a single cell dividing to flowers attracting bees—discover how life creates new life.

characters.name: Asha
characters.role: farmer's daughter noticing reproduction in nature

slides.title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
slides.storyContext: Asha watches her mother's plants grow, flowers bloom, and fruits appear. She wonders: where do new plants and animals come from?

image.alt: How do Organisms Reproduce? — How do Organisms Reproduce?

slides.title: Life Begets Life
slides.storyContext: On the farm, Asha notices apple trees produce thousands of seeds, bacteria in milk spoil the yogurt overnight, and the bullfrog in the pond croaks during monsoon. Ravi asks: 'Why do all living things make copies of themselves?' Professor Gupta smiles and begins the lesson.

image.alt: Life Begets Life — How do Organisms Reproduce?

slides.title: Why Reproduce?
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta explains: 'Reproduction isn't just about making babies. It's how life continues despite predators, disease, and accidents. It's survival.'

points.label: Characteristics of reproduction
points.text: Produces new organisms. Passes genetic material (DNA) to offspring. Increases population size.

points.label: Two modes
points.text: Asexual: one parent, genetically identical offspring (clones). Sexual: two parents, genetically unique offspring.

points.label: Evolutionary advantage
points.text: Sexual reproduction creates variation. Variation means some offspring survive new environments better (natural selection).

example.problem: Bacteria divide asexually every 20 minutes. Humans reproduce sexually, taking 9 months. Why might sexual reproduction be slower but more successful for complex organisms?
example.solution: Bacteria benefit from rapid asexual reproduction to colonize resources. Humans benefit from sexual reproduction because genetic variation provides insurance against disease and environmental change. A single mutation in a bacterium can affect a billion clones; in humans, genetic diversity buffers this risk.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reproduction makes new life. Asexual reproduction is fast but makes copies. Sexual reproduction is slower but creates unique offspring.

image.alt: Why Reproduce? — How do Organisms Reproduce?

slides.title: Asha's Farm Observations
slides.storyContext: Asha watches bacteria bloom in a petri dish, potato eyes sprout into plants, and frogs lay eggs that hatch into tadpoles. 'Three different ways to make life,' she observes. Professor Gupta nods. 'And each way fits the organism's life.'

slides.title: Asexual Reproduction
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta picks up a potato with an eye. 'This potato can grow into a new plant with just a cutting. No need for a partner.'

points.label: Binary fission (Bacteria/Prokaryotes)
points.text: One cell replicates DNA and splits into two identical daughter cells. E.g., E. coli divides every 20 minutes.

points.label: Budding (Yeast/Hydra)
points.text: Parent organism grows an outgrowth (bud). Bud detaches and becomes a new organism.

points.label: Fragmentation (Starfish/Planaria)
points.text: Parent breaks into pieces. Each piece regenerates into a complete organism.

points.label: Vegetative propagation (Plants)
points.text: Runners (strawberry), tubers (potato), bulbs (onion), fragmentation (bryophyllum leaf). No seeds involved.

example.problem: A gardener cuts a rose stem and plants it in soil. After weeks, it grows roots and becomes a new rose plant. Is this sexual or asexual reproduction? Why?
example.solution: Asexual (vegetative propagation). Only one parent (the original rose). No gametes (sex cells) are involved. The new plant is genetically identical (a clone) to the parent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Asexual reproduction means one parent makes babies that are exact copies (clones). Plants can do this from a leaf or stem cutting.

image.alt: Asexual Reproduction — How do Organisms Reproduce?

slides.title: Binary Fission in Bacteria
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta shows a time-lapse video of bacteria multiplying. 'Watch how one cell becomes two, then four, then eight, in just hours.'

example.problem: A single E. coli bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting at 1 PM, how many bacteria will there be by 3 PM (2 hours)?
example.solution: 2 hours = 120 minutes. Number of divisions = 120 / 20 = 6. Number of bacteria = 2^6 = 64. From one bacterium to 64 in 2 hours!

slides.title: Sexual Reproduction: The Flower
slides.storyContext: Asha observes the marigolds in her garden. 'Look at the pollen on the bee,' Professor Gupta points out. 'That's the plant's way of bringing two parents together.'

points.label: Flower structure
points.text: Stamen (male): anther (produces pollen with sperm), filament (support). Pistil (female): stigma (receives pollen), style, ovary (contains ovules with egg).

points.label: Pollination
points.text: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. Vectors: bees (insects), wind, water, or self-pollination.

points.label: Fertilization
points.text: Pollen tube grows down style into ovule. Sperm nucleus fuses with egg nucleus. Diploid zygote forms.

points.label: Fruit and seed
points.text: Ovary develops into fruit (for seed dispersal). Ovule develops into seed (contains embryo and food store).

example.problem: A flower is pollinated by a bee. Trace the journey from pollen to seed.
example.solution: 1. Pollen (with sperm) from one flower's anther lands on another flower's stigma (pollination). 2. Pollen tube grows down the style. 3. Sperm nucleus travels down the pollen tube into the ovule. 4. Sperm and egg fuse (fertilization), forming a zygote. 5. Zygote develops into embryo; ovule develops into seed. 6. Ovary swells into fruit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pollen (boy part) from one flower lands on the stigma (girl part) of another. They merge, and seeds form in the fruit.

image.alt: Sexual Reproduction: The Flower — How do Organisms Reproduce?

slides.title: Asha Watches the Bees
slides.storyContext: Asha sits by the sunflowers and watches bees land, collect pollen, and fly to the next flower. 'They're not just getting food,' Professor Gupta says. 'They're matchmakers for plants.'

slides.title: Gametes and Meiosis
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta draws. 'Before a plant can reproduce sexually, it must create special cells called gametes. In plants, we call them spores; in animals, sperm and egg.'

points.label: Gamete definition
points.text: Specialized sex cell (haploid, n) that fuses with another gamete. Sperm (male) or egg/ovum (female).

points.label: Meiosis
points.text: Cell division that produces gametes. Starts with diploid cell (2n), produces four haploid cells (n).

points.label: Haploid vs. diploid
points.text: Haploid (n): one set of chromosomes. Diploid (2n): two sets (one from each parent). Fertilization (n + n) restores diploid in offspring.

example.problem: An apple tree cell is diploid (2n = 34, for example). It undergoes meiosis to produce pollen. Each pollen grain's sperm nucleus is haploid (n = 17). When two pollen grains (sperm, n = 17 each) fuse with two egg cells (n = 17 each), what is the diploid number of the seed?
example.solution: Each resulting seed is diploid (2n = 34). Sperm (n = 17) + egg (n = 17) = zygote (2n = 34).

slides.inSimpleWords: Gametes are sex cells with half the chromosomes. When they merge, the baby gets a full set again.

slides.title: Sexual Reproduction in Animals: Human Reproduction
slides.storyContext: Ravi blushes as Professor Gupta discusses human reproduction matter-of-factly. 'This is biology. Every human starts as a union of two cells.'

points.label: Gametogenesis
points.text: Spermatogenesis (testes): produces sperm (n). Oogenesis (ovary): produces egg/ovum (n). Both haploid gametes.

points.label: Fertilization
points.text: Sperm (n) + Egg (n) → Zygote (2n). Occurs in fallopian tube.

points.label: Pregnancy
points.text: Zygote divides (mitosis) → blastocyst → implants in uterus wall. Placenta exchanges nutrients and O₂ between fetus and mother. Lasts ~40 weeks (9 months).

points.label: Birth
points.text: Uterine contractions expel the fetus. Umbilical cord cut. Newborn breathes air for the first time.

example.problem: A couple's baby is born with blue eyes, though both parents have brown eyes. How is this possible?
example.solution: Blue eye color is recessive. Both parents carry the recessive allele (b) along with dominant brown allele (B). They are Bb. The baby inherited b from each parent (bb), expressing blue eyes. (See next chapter: Heredity.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Sperm and egg merge to make a zygote, which grows into a baby in the mother's womb for 9 months, then is born.

image.alt: Sexual Reproduction in Animals: Human Reproduction — How do Organisms Reproduce?

slides.title: The Journey of a Sperm
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta animates. 'A sperm swims from the vagina, through the cervix, into the uterus, up the fallopian tube. Millions try; only one succeeds. It's a race.'

slides.title: Meiosis: The Sex Cell Division
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta draws a diagram. 'To create gametes (sperm and egg), cells must divide differently. They halve their chromosomes.'

points.label: Meiosis
points.text: Two divisions (Meiosis I, Meiosis II). Produces four haploid (n) cells from one diploid (2n) cell.

points.label: Meiosis I (Reduction division)
points.text: Homologous chromosomes separate. Each daughter cell gets one of each pair. Crossing over increases variation.

points.label: Meiosis II (Mitotic division)
points.text: Sister chromatids separate, like mitosis. Produces four non-identical haploid cells.

points.label: Variation
points.text: Crossing over and independent assortment ensure genetic diversity in gametes.

example.problem: A man produces sperm via meiosis. Each sperm is genetically unique (even among his own sperm). Why?
example.solution: During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes assort independently. During crossing over, genes are exchanged between homologs. Each sperm gets a random combination of chromosomes and recombined genes, ensuring uniqueness.

slides.inSimpleWords: Meiosis is special division that makes sex cells. It cuts the chromosome number in half and mixes genes so each gamete is different.

image.alt: Meiosis: The Sex Cell Division — How do Organisms Reproduce?

slides.title: Mitosis vs. Meiosis
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta contrasts the two types of division side-by-side.

example.problem: A skin cell (diploid, 2n = 46) undergoes mitosis. A sperm-producing cell also has 2n = 46 and undergoes meiosis. How do the products differ in number and genetics?
example.solution: Mitosis: 46 → 46, 46 (two identical daughter cells, both diploid). Meiosis: 46 → 23, 23, 23, 23 (four non-identical daughter cells, all haploid). Mitosis maintains genetic identity; meiosis creates variation and halves chromosome number for gamete formation.

slides.title: Full Example: From Flower to Seed
slides.storyContext: Asha tracks a sunflower from bloom to seed-bearing head.

example.problem: A sunflower blooms in summer. A bee pollinates it. The seed develops and is dispersed by wind. Trace the entire reproductive cycle, including the roles of meiosis, pollination, and fertilization.
example.solution: 1. Anthers undergo meiosis, producing pollen grains (male gametophyte, haploid sperm). 2. Ovary undergoes meiosis, producing ovules (female gametophyte, haploid egg). 3. Bee lands on sunflower, collecting pollen on its body. 4. Bee visits another sunflower, pollinating the stigma. 5. Pollen tube grows down style. Sperm nucleus (n) fuses with egg nucleus (n), forming zygote (2n). 6. Zygote develops into seed embryo. Ovule becomes seed coat. Ovary becomes fruit (seed shell). 7. Seed is dispersed by wind, germinates in soil, and grows into a new plant.

image.alt: Full Example: From Flower to Seed — How do Organisms Reproduce?

slides.title: Challenge: Comparing Two Parents
slides.storyContext: Ravi compares two potatoes—one grown from a cutting (asexual) and one grown from a seed (sexual).

example.problem: Potato A was grown from a cutting of Potato X (asexual reproduction). Potato B grew from a seed produced by Potato X and Potato Y (sexual reproduction). How do A and B differ genetically? If a disease kills Potato X, predict which farm (growing A or B) is more vulnerable.
example.solution: Potato A is genetically identical to Potato X (clone). Potato B is genetically unique—it carries genes from both X and Y. If a disease kills Potato X, the farm growing only clones of X (Potato A) will suffer total loss. The farm with B has more genetic diversity and some plants may carry resistance genes.

image.alt: Challenge: Comparing Two Parents — How do Organisms Reproduce?

slides.title: Challenge: Pollination Strategy
slides.storyContext: Two plants compete in the same meadow. One produces bright red flowers and sweet nectar; the other produces small green flowers and relies on wind.

example.problem: Which plant is using insect pollination and which is using wind pollination? How do their flower structures differ? Which strategy is more reliable in a pollinator-poor year?
example.solution: Red flowers with nectar = insect (bee, butterfly) pollination. Green flowers = wind pollination. Red flowers invest energy in attracting insects; wind pollination is passive and relies on air currents, not pollinators. In a pollinator-poor year, the wind-pollinated plant has the advantage. But if wind is rare and still, insects are more reliable.

slides.title: Challenge: Asexual Crops & Genetic Vulnerability
slides.storyContext: Many crops like bananas and cassava are grown asexually (from cuttings) to preserve desirable traits.

example.problem: Banana crops worldwide are genetically identical clones. A new fungal disease emerges that kills this variety. Explain why the impact is so severe and what strategies could reduce vulnerability in the future.
example.solution: All bananas share identical genetics, so all are equally susceptible. The disease wipes out the entire crop. Future strategies: (1) develop sexually-reproduced banana lines (outcrossing with wild relatives for genetic diversity), (2) rotate between different varieties, (3) implement disease-resistance breeding programs, (4) quarantine practices to slow disease spread.

slides.title: Seed Dispersal in Nature
slides.storyContext: Asha watches seeds drift on the wind and animals eating fruits and spreading seeds far away. 'After flowers and fruit come seeds. And seeds find new soil, new homes, new forests.'

slides.title: Types of Seed Dispersal
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta categorizes. 'Seeds travel by wind, water, or animals. Each method shapes the seed's design.'

example.problem: A maple tree produces winged seeds. A coconut tree produces floating seeds. An apple tree produces seeds in juicy fruit. How does the seed design match the dispersal method?
example.solution: Maple (wind): lightweight seeds with wings for gliding. Coconut (water): thick, waterproof husk for buoyancy and long ocean journeys. Apple (animal): soft, nutritious fruit attracts birds and mammals; they eat, digest, and scatter seeds via droppings far from parent.

slides.title: Challenge: Regeneration and Cloning
slides.storyContext: A starfish loses an arm to a predator but grows it back. A planarian worm is cut in half and both halves regenerate into complete worms.

example.problem: Starfish can lose multiple arms and regenerate them (asexual reproduction via fragmentation). This organism is essentially cloning itself. What are the evolutionary advantages and disadvantages of regeneration as a reproductive strategy?
example.solution: Advantage: rapid population growth without finding a mate; increases survival if predators remove limbs. Disadvantage: genetic uniformity; if a disease or environmental change kills one, all clones suffer; no genetic variation for evolution. Best for stable environments; risky during ecological upheaval.

slides.title: Life Cycle Diversity
slides.storyContext: Ravi reflects. 'A bacterium lives one day. A mayfly lives one day. A human lives eighty years. A sequoia lives three thousand years. But all reproduce. All pass on their genes.'

slides.title: Environmental Triggers for Reproduction
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta describes. 'Many organisms time their reproduction to environmental signals—day length, temperature, rainfall.'

example.problem: Frogs in a monsoon pond don't croak year-round. They croak during the monsoon rains. How might rainfall trigger reproductive behavior? Why is timing reproduction to rainfall adaptive?
example.solution: Rainfall increases water in ponds and provides food (insects, plants). Tadpoles are more likely to survive to metamorphosis. Temperature changes and noise from rain may trigger hormonal cascades (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) that activate reproductive behavior. Adaptation: timing reproduction to abundant resources ensures offspring have food and shelter.

slides.title: The Trade-off: Speed vs. Diversity
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks Professor Gupta. 'If asexual reproduction is faster, why do sexually-reproducing organisms even exist?' Professor Gupta smiles. 'Because in a changing world, diversity saves species.'

slides.title: Double Fertilization in Flowering Plants
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta reveals an advanced detail. 'Flowering plants have a trick—double fertilization—not found in other plants.'

example.problem: In a flowering plant, one sperm nucleus (n) fuses with the egg (n), forming the embryo (2n). But the pollen grain has TWO sperm nuclei. Where does the second sperm nucleus go and what does it form?
example.solution: The second sperm nucleus fuses with two polar nuclei (n + n) in the central cell, forming the endosperm (3n—triploid). The endosperm becomes the nutritive tissue inside the seed that feeds the developing embryo. This is double fertilization, unique to flowering plants and highly efficient.

slides.title: From Flower to Fruit
slides.storyContext: Asha watches the transformation. 'The flower withers. But inside, the ovary swells, ripens, changes color and sweetness. The fruit that protects seeds is also designed to be eaten, to be spread.'

slides.title: Summary: Reproduction—Life's Continuation
slides.storyContext: Professor Gupta concludes: 'Asexual reproduction is fast but risky. Sexual reproduction is slow but wise. Together, life persists.'

points.label: Asexual reproduction
points.text: One parent, genetically identical offspring (clones). Faster. Examples: fission, budding, vegetative propagation.

points.label: Sexual reproduction
points.text: Two parents, genetically unique offspring. Slower but creates variation. Gametes form via meiosis.

points.label: Gametes and meiosis
points.text: Meiosis produces haploid gametes (sperm, egg, pollen) from diploid cells. Reduces chromosome number by half.

points.label: Flower reproduction
points.text: Pollination + fertilization → seed + fruit. Pollinator vectors (bees, wind) transfer pollen.

points.label: Human reproduction
points.text: Sperm + Egg → Zygote → Fetus (9 months in womb) → Birth.

points.label: Meiosis and variation
points.text: Crossing over and independent assortment increase genetic variation in gametes.

points.label: Evolutionary insight
points.text: Genetic variation from sexual reproduction allows populations to adapt to changing environments.

subject: Biology
title: Heredity: Genes, Chromosomes & Inheritance
hook: Why do you look like your parents? Why do some traits skip a generation? Explore Mendel's laws and DNA.

characters.name: Dev
characters.role: curious student wondering why he looks like his father

slides.title: Heredity
slides.storyContext: Dev notices he has his father's curly hair and his mother's brown eyes. He wonders: why do children inherit traits? What's the blueprint?

image.alt: Heredity — Heredity

slides.title: Why Do We Look Like Our Parents?
slides.storyContext: At a family gathering, Grandma Savitri points to Dev's curly hair. 'Like your father,' she smiles. 'And your mother's kindness.' Dev asks Miss Malini: 'How does that work?' Miss Malini brings out Mendel's pea plants and begins the journey into heredity.

image.alt: Why Do We Look Like Our Parents? — Heredity

slides.title: DNA, Genes, and Chromosomes
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini draws a nested diagram. 'Think of it like a library. Chromosomes are the books. Genes are the chapters. DNA is the language.'

points.label: DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid)
points.text: Double helix molecule. Carries genetic instructions. Made of nucleotides (bases A, T, G, C). Base pairing: A-T, G-C.

points.label: Gene
points.text: A segment of DNA that codes for a specific protein or trait. Humans have ~20,000 genes.

points.label: Chromosome
points.text: A structure of tightly coiled DNA and proteins. Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). One pair (sex chromosomes: XX or XY) determines sex.

points.label: Allele
points.text: Alternative forms of a gene. E.g., allele for curly hair (C) and allele for straight hair (c).

example.problem: A human cell nucleus contains 46 chromosomes. A sperm cell contains 23. Explain.
example.solution: Body cells (somatic cells) are diploid (2n = 46): 23 pairs. Sperm and egg (gametes) are haploid (n = 23): one of each pair. During meiosis, chromosome number is halved.

slides.inSimpleWords: DNA is the instruction manual for your body. Genes are specific instructions on DNA. Chromosomes are packages of DNA. You inherit DNA from both parents.

image.alt: DNA, Genes, and Chromosomes — Heredity

slides.title: Dev's DNA Heritage
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini explains. 'Dev, you have 23 chromosome pairs. 23 from your father, 23 from your mother. They overlap, blend, combine. That's why you're partly him, partly her, and wholly you.'

slides.title: DNA Structure and Replication
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini draws the double helix. 'DNA isn't just storage. It copies itself every time a cell divides. It's a self-replicating blueprint.'

points.label: Double helix shape
points.text: Two strands of nucleotides twisted around each other. Bases pair: A with T, G with C (complementary base pairing).

points.label: Nucleotides
points.text: Building blocks of DNA. Each has a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base (A, T, G, or C).

points.label: DNA replication
points.text: The two strands separate. Each serves as a template. New complementary strands are built. Result: two identical DNA molecules (semi-conservative replication).

points.label: Central dogma
points.text: DNA → RNA → Protein. Genes code for proteins; proteins determine traits.

example.problem: A DNA strand reads A-T-G-C-A-T. What does its complementary strand read?
example.solution: T-A-C-G-T-A. A pairs with T, T pairs with A, G pairs with C, C pairs with G.

slides.inSimpleWords: DNA is two strands twisted together. Each strand holds instructions written in a 4-letter code (A, T, G, C). When DNA copies itself, each strand guides building a new twin strand.

slides.title: Gregor Mendel & the Laws of Inheritance
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini holds up a small portrait. 'This is Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk in the 1860s. He grew pea plants and discovered the rules of inheritance.'

points.label: Mendel's First Law (Law of Segregation)
points.text: Alleles for a trait separate during gamete formation. Each gamete receives ONE allele. Offspring get alleles from both parents.

points.label: Mendel's Second Law (Law of Independent Assortment)
points.text: Alleles of different genes assort independently. Inheritance of one trait does not affect another (for genes on different chromosomes).

points.label: Dominant vs. Recessive
points.text: Dominant allele (D) masks recessive allele (d). DD or Dd = dominant phenotype. dd = recessive phenotype.

example.problem: Mendel crossed tall pea plants (TT) with short pea plants (tt). All F1 offspring were tall. Why?
example.solution: F1 offspring are all Tt (heterozygous). T (tall, dominant) masks t (short, recessive). Phenotype is tall. In F2 (Tt × Tt), the ratio is 3 tall (TT, Tt, Tt) to 1 short (tt).

slides.inSimpleWords: Mendel found that traits follow patterns. Some traits hide and some show. Children get one gene from each parent for each trait.

image.alt: Gregor Mendel & the Laws of Inheritance — Heredity

slides.title: Mendel's Pea Experiment
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini narrates. 'Mendel took tall peas and short peas. He let them breed. The tall reappeared. Then he let those breed. Tall and short both returned. He'd discovered the hidden patterns of heredity.'

slides.title: Monohybrid Cross: A Worked Example
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini sets up a Punnett square on the board. 'Let's trace one trait—eye color. Dev, your mother is Bb (brown eyes, carrier of blue). Your father is Bb. What's your chance of blue eyes?'

points.label: Phenotype vs. Genotype
points.text: Genotype: genetic makeup (Bb). Phenotype: observable trait (brown eyes).

points.label: Punnett square
points.text: Tool to predict offspring ratios. Each parent's alleles (columns/rows) × each other. Four boxes = four possible offspring.

points.label: Monohybrid cross
points.text: Tracking ONE trait across generations. Parental cross → F1 → F2 shows segregation.

points.label: Probability
points.text: Each offspring has a 25% chance for each genotype combination. Ratios are statistical; actual outcomes vary with sample size.

example.problem: Dev's parents are both Bb (brown eyes). Set up a Punnett square. What are the possible genotypes and phenotypes of their children?
example.solution: Punnett square: BB, Bb, Bb, bb. Genotypes: 1 BB, 2 Bb, 1 bb. Phenotypes: 3 brown (BB, Bb, Bb), 1 blue (bb). Ratio 3:1 (brown:blue). Dev could be BB, Bb, or bb.

slides.inSimpleWords: A Punnett square shows all possible combinations of genes from two parents. Each cell is one possible child.

image.alt: Monohybrid Cross: A Worked Example — Heredity

slides.title: Working a Punnett Square Step-by-Step
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini guides Dev through the process on the board.

example.problem: Two heterozygous brown-eyed parents (Bb) have a baby. What is the probability the baby has blue eyes (bb)?
example.solution: Step 1: List parent genotypes. Parent 1: Bb. Parent 2: Bb. Step 2: Draw Punnett square (2x2 grid). Top = B, b. Left = B, b. Step 3: Fill in combinations: BB, Bb, Bb, bb. Step 4: Count bb = 1 out of 4. Probability = 25% or 1/4.

slides.title: Sex Determination & Sex-Linked Traits
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini points to Dev's older sister. 'Your sister is XX. You are XY. That Y chromosome comes only from your father, determining that you are male.'

points.label: Sex chromosomes
points.text: XX = female. XY = male. Females have two X alleles for any trait on the X chromosome. Males have only one (hemizygous).

points.label: Sex-linked traits
points.text: Genes on the X chromosome. Males are more likely to express recessive X-linked traits (only one copy).

points.label: Color blindness example
points.text: Red-green color blindness is X-linked recessive. XᶜXᶜ female (colorblind), XᶜX female (carrier), XX female (normal). Xᶜ Y male (colorblind), XY male (normal).

points.label: Inheritance pattern
points.text: Colorblind males likely pass the allele to daughters (who become carriers). Carrier mothers have 50% chance of colorblind sons.

example.problem: A colorblind man (Xᶜ Y) and a carrier woman (Xᶜ X) have a daughter. What is her genotype and phenotype?
example.solution: Punnett square: Xᶜ Xᶜ (colorblind) or Xᶜ X (carrier, normal vision). 50% chance of each. Daughters cannot receive Y from father, only Xᶜ.

slides.inSimpleWords: The X and Y chromosomes determine sex. Traits on the X chromosome show differently in males (one copy) and females (two copies).

image.alt: Sex Determination & Sex-Linked Traits — Heredity

slides.title: Why Color Blindness Runs in Families
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini explains. 'Color blindness is rare in women but common in men. Why? The gene is on the X chromosome. Men have only one X; if it carries the allele, they're colorblind. Women need two copies, which is rare.'

slides.title: Multiple Alleles and Polygenic Traits
slides.storyContext: Grandma Savitri comments: 'Dev, your skin tone is different from both your mother and father. That's because many genes control it, not just one.'

points.label: Multiple alleles
points.text: A gene can have MORE than two alleles in a population. Example: ABO blood type has A, B, O alleles.

points.label: ABO blood type
points.text: Iᴬ Iᴬ or Iᴬ i = A. Iᴮ Iᴮ or Iᴮ i = B. Iᴬ Iᴮ = AB. ii = O.

points.label: Codominance
points.text: Both alleles express equally. E.g., AB blood type shows both A and B antigens.

points.label: Polygenic traits
points.text: Multiple genes control one trait (skin color, height, intelligence). Offspring show continuous variation, not discrete categories.

example.problem: A man with blood type A (Iᴬ i) and a woman with blood type B (Iᴮ i) have children. What blood types are possible?
example.solution: Punnett square: Iᴬ Iᴮ (AB), Iᴬ i (A), Iᴮ i (B), ii (O). Possible children: A, B, AB, or O.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some genes have many versions. Skin color, height, and intelligence are controlled by many genes working together, so people vary widely.

image.alt: Multiple Alleles and Polygenic Traits — Heredity

slides.title: Blood Type Inheritance
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini shows a chart of blood types. 'Blood type is a great example of multiple alleles and codominance.'

example.problem: A woman with AB blood type and a man with O blood type have a child. What are the possible blood types?
example.solution: Woman is Iᴬ Iᴮ. Man is ii. Cross: Iᴬ i (type A) or Iᴮ i (type B). Children can be type A or type B, but not AB or O.

slides.title: Full Example: Dev's Inheritance Pattern
slides.storyContext: Dev learns his full genetic story by analyzing his own traits against his parents' and grandparents'.

example.problem: Dev has curly hair (C, dominant), brown eyes (B, dominant), and blood type AB. His father has curly hair, brown eyes, and blood type A. His mother has straight hair, brown eyes, and blood type B. Determine: (a) Dev's genotype for each trait. (b) His parents' genotypes. (c) The probability that Dev's sister is colorblind (X-linked recessive) if his mother is a carrier.
example.solution: (a) Dev: Curly hair (C_, genotype Cc or CC), Brown eyes (B_, likely Bb), Blood type AB (Iᴬ Iᴮ). (b) Father: Cc (curly), Bb (brown), Iᴬ i (type A). Mother: cc (straight), Bb (brown), Iᴮ i (type B). (c) Sister: 50% chance carrier (Xᶜ X, normal vision), 50% chance normal (XX, normal vision). 0% chance colorblind (would need Xᶜ Xᶜ, but father is normal XY, so cannot pass Xᶜ).

image.alt: Full Example: Dev's Inheritance Pattern — Heredity

slides.title: Challenge: Genetic Counseling
slides.storyContext: Dev's cousin is getting married. She learns that her fiancé's family has a history of hemophilia (X-linked recessive bleeding disorder). She is a carrier (Xʰ X).

example.problem: Dev's cousin (Xʰ X, carrier for hemophilia) and her fiancé (XY, normal) are planning to have children. What are the possible outcomes for sons and daughters?
example.solution: Punnett square: Daughters: XX (normal) or Xʰ X (carrier). Sons: XY (normal) or Xʰ Y (hemophilic). 50% of daughters will be carriers. 50% of sons will have hemophilia. No daughter will be affected (father contributes normal X). All daughters have at least one Xʰ chance.

image.alt: Challenge: Genetic Counseling — Heredity

slides.title: Challenge: Two-Trait Inheritance
slides.storyContext: Dev studies tomato plants where round fruit (R) is dominant to oval (r) and red color (C) is dominant to yellow (c).

example.problem: A round-red tomato (RrCc) self-pollinates. What are the expected phenotypes and their ratios in the offspring?
example.solution: Dihybrid cross: RrCc × RrCc. Expected phenotypes: 9 round-red (R_C_), 3 round-yellow (R_cc), 3 oval-red (rrC_), 1 oval-yellow (rrcc). Ratio 9:3:3:1. (This is the classic dihybrid ratio demonstrating independent assortment.)

slides.title: Challenge: Trait Inheritance Across Generations
slides.storyContext: Grandma Savitri's father had red hair (recessive, rr), but Grandma has brown hair (R_). Grandma's husband also had brown hair (R_).

example.problem: Grandma Savitri (brown hair, R_) is the child of a red-haired father (rr). What is Grandma's genotype? If Grandma's son (Dev's grandfather) has red hair, what does that tell us about Grandma's husband's genotype? Could their daughter (Dev's mother) have red hair if she married a red-haired man?
example.solution: Grandma's genotype: Rr (must carry recessive from her red-haired father). Grandfather's genotype: must be at least rr or r_ (if he has red-haired children with Grandma, he must carry r). Dev's mother: If grandfather is rr, then mother is Rr (could have red hair if married to rr man). If grandfather is Rr, then mother is 50% Rr, 50% rr (rr mother + rr father = rr child, so yes, red hair possible).

slides.title: Genetic Variation in Families
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini describes. 'In a family of four siblings, each is genetically unique. Their parents shuffled genes differently for each child. That's why siblings can look so different—or so alike.'

slides.title: Crossing Over and Genetic Recombination
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini animates meiosis. 'During meiosis, chromosomes don't just separate. They exchange pieces—crossing over. This shuffles genes on the same chromosome.'

example.problem: A chromosome from Dev's mother carries alleles: A-B-C (for three linked genes). Dev's father's chromosome carries: a-b-c. During meiosis in the mother, crossing over swaps the middle section: A-b-C. What new allele combinations can Dev inherit?
example.solution: Without crossing over, Dev would get either A-B-C or normal chromosomes from mother. With crossing over, new combinations like A-b-C are possible. This is recombination. Each gamete can carry novel allele combinations that weren't in either parent—genetic innovation.

slides.title: Challenge: Carrier States and Genetic Disease
slides.storyContext: Cystic fibrosis is a recessive genetic disease. Two carrier parents (Cc) want to have children and ask about risks.

example.problem: Two carrier parents (Cc) for cystic fibrosis have a child together. (a) What is the probability the child has the disease (cc)? (b) What is the probability the child is a carrier but healthy (Cc)? (c) What if they have three children—what are the chances that at least one has CF?
example.solution: (a) 25% (1/4 chance cc). (b) 50% (2/4 chance Cc). (c) P(at least one CF) = 1 - P(none CF). P(child is not cc) = 3/4 per child. P(none CF in 3 children) = (3/4)^3 = 27/64. P(at least one CF) = 1 - 27/64 = 37/64 ≈ 58%.

slides.title: Evolution and Heredity
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini concludes. 'Heredity isn't just about copying parents. With sexual reproduction, mutations, and natural selection, life evolves. Traits that help survival spread through a population. Over generations, new species arise.'

slides.title: Mutations: Errors and Opportunities
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini explains. 'Rarely, DNA copying errors occur—mutations. Some are harmful. Some are neutral. Some are beneficial.'

example.problem: A mutation changes a mosquito's genotype, allowing it to survive insecticide. Before the mutation, the population had allele p (susceptible). After mutation, allele P (resistant) arises. How does natural selection act? Which allele increases in frequency over generations, and why?
example.solution: Initially, p is common, P is rare. Insecticide is applied: pp and pP individuals die; PP individuals survive and reproduce. P allele frequency increases each generation because carriers survive and pass P to offspring. Eventually, P becomes common, p becomes rare. The population has evolved resistance to insecticide. This is evolution by natural selection.

slides.title: You Are a Combination
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini looks at Dev. 'You inherited genes from your parents, grandparents, great-grandparents. You're a living mosaic of thousands of ancestors. And that makes you unique.'

slides.title: The Human Genome Project
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini explains. 'Scientists mapped all ~20,000 human genes and 3 billion base pairs of DNA. The results showed we share 99.9% of our DNA—yet that 0.1% accounts for all human diversity.'

example.problem: If two humans differ by only 0.1% of 3 billion base pairs, how many base pairs differ between any two individuals? Why is this tiny difference enough to make every person unique?
example.solution: 0.1% of 3 billion = 3 million base pairs differ between any two humans. This variation is distributed across thousands of genes. With billions of possible combinations from sexual reproduction (recombination, independent assortment), the probability two siblings share identical genotypes is vanishingly small. That's why you're unique.

slides.title: Grandma's Wisdom
slides.storyContext: Grandma Savitri smiles at Dev. 'Your grandfather's eyes, your mother's laugh, your father's strength. You carry all of us forward. That's the gift of heredity—you're never alone.'

slides.title: Summary: Heredity—The Science of Inheritance
slides.storyContext: Miss Malini concludes: 'Now you understand. You are not a copy of your parents. You are a unique blend of their genes, and that blend makes you irreplaceably you.'

points.label: DNA structure
points.text: Double helix of nucleotides (A, T, G, C). Complementary base pairing. Self-replicating.

points.label: Genes and chromosomes
points.text: Genes are DNA segments. Chromosomes package DNA. Humans have 46 (23 pairs). One pair (sex chromosomes) determines sex.

points.label: Mendel's laws
points.text: Law of Segregation: alleles separate in gametes. Law of Independent Assortment: different genes assort independently.

points.label: Dominant & recessive
points.text: Dominant alleles mask recessive. Phenotype depends on genotype and dominance.

points.label: Monohybrid cross
points.text: Punnett square tracks one trait. 3:1 ratio in F2 if both parents are heterozygous.

points.label: Sex-linked traits
points.text: Genes on X chromosome show differently in males (one copy) and females (two copies). Males express recessive X-linked traits more often.

points.label: Multiple alleles & polygenic
points.text: Some genes have >2 versions (ABO blood). Multiple genes control continuous traits (height, skin color).

image.alt: Summary: Heredity—The Science of Inheritance — Heredity
